E0919.summary: An adept whom Atwood cites as having reportedly possessed the Powder; she judges his book weak and his lavishness blameworthy, but uses his verses on the Art coming by grace.
E0919.body: Atwood names Kelly, author of *De Lapide Philosophorum*, as an adept who reportedly possessed the Powder, but she judges his book of little value and criticizes his lavishness [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶67]. Elsewhere she cites Kelly’s verses in Ashmole’s *Theatrum* in support of her view that the Art is not obtained by reading or by will: “by grace it is obtained” [IV.1 ¶19; IV.1 n19].

E0920.summary: The decisive secret that opens the Mystery and the Art; also, among the authorities, the name for successive numbered operations of the practice and for explanatory texts.
E0920.body:
**Atwood's usage.** For Atwood the Key is what opens the Mystery and alone passes its wards: without it the Mystery can neither be entered nor explained, and with it the Adepts' writings become instructive — “If, however, the Key is wanting, how may we presume to enter” [IV.4 ¶32]. She identifies it with Light: “the Key thereof is Light” [IV.4 ¶32]. Even holding it does not guarantee more than entry to the vestibule when the texts are scrambled, “even to those who had already become possessed of the true key” [I.1 ¶82]. The Alchemists “delivered many Keys, whereby, as they say, we may enter into the sanctuary of philosophy”, but these do not unfold the first approach [IV.1 ¶3]. She also calls the six texts she then presents Keys: “The six following Keys, delivered into the safe hand of the intelligent inquirer” [IV.2 ¶45].

**Quoted authorities.** Basil Valentine, with Kirchringius and Madathan, makes the key the decisive secret, opening the first and the last gate, so that missing it ruins the whole course: “this key is the principal part of the whole Art; this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last” [III.1 ¶37]. Eudoxus uses Keys for six successive, numbered operations, each ending at a stated point — the First at the whitening of the Stone, the Second at digestion and putrefaction — and placed within works: “the operation of the Second Key of the First Work is ended” [IV.3 ¶5]. He also speaks of the Fourth, Fifth and Sixth Keys, and says that whoever knows the Stone and Our Fire has “the Keys of the Art”; the mercurial liquor is “the Key of our Art” [IV.3 ¶16].

The records thus show two senses: a single decisive secret (Atwood, Basil Valentine), and a sequence of operational stages or texts (Eudoxus; Atwood's six Keys).

E0921.summary: Held by the one competent to minister, who opens and no man shuts; Atwood does not explain it further.
E0921.body: Atwood says the one competent to minister is “he that hath the Key of David”, who opens and no man shuts [IV.3 ¶39]. The text gives no further explanation. Compare the Appendix's “Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97] (see Key to the Work).

E0922.summary: In a passage quoted from Hermes, the ferment's action of whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies.
E0922.body: Quoting Hermes, Atwood gives the ferment's action — whitening, protecting, holding the tincture and joining the bodies — and Hermes says “this is the Key of the philosophers and the end of their works” [I.3 ¶58].

E0923.summary: In the Master's words, the dissolution of the composition by the power of the Water.
E0923.body: In a passage given as the Master's, the dissolution of the composition by the Water is named: “when by the power of the Water the composition is dissolved, it is the Key of the Restoration” [IV.2 ¶14].

E0924.summary: In the Appendix, entry into the work or into another life, gained when the desire of the lower life opens into the heart life by exstasis.
E0924.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood says the entry into the work, or into another life, is gained from the desire of the lower life opening into the heart life by exstasis. She equates it with the Key of the House of David: “The Key to the Work, or into another life, the Key of the House of David” [APP ¶97].

E0925.summary: Something “rejected” that regains “her Head place” only after the labours of the Heroic Intellect; the text does not decode it.
E0925.body: Atwood writes of the labours of the Heroic Intellect, which must come “before the rejected Keystone regains her Head place” [II.2 ¶29]. The text does not say plainly what the Keystone is.

E0926.summary: A pious German adept, author of the *Ampitheatrum Sapientae Eternae*, whom Atwood treats as a main authority on the Azoth, the Stone's virtues, and the practice.
E0926.body:
Atwood lists Henry Khunrath among the German adepts, a pious adept embittered by mistreatment; works named include the *Ampitheat. Sapientiae Eternae* and *Magnesia Catholica* [I.1 ¶66; I.1 ¶70; I.1 n84].

**What she takes from him (endorsed).**
- The Azoth as tangible; he received the universal tincture and healed with it, and argued against self-deception: “I write not fables” [I.1 ¶81; I.1 n106]. He cites an ancient author on the perpetually burning ether: “the ether in this praeter-perfect aqueous body will burn perpetually” [I.1 ¶20; I.1 n28].
- The threefold secret, separation, no manual labour, the Azoth, and the colour sequence ending in the glorified Stone: “Seek Three in One, and again seek One in Three, dissolve, congeal” [III.3 ¶9; III.3 n3; III.3 ¶19; III.3 n11].
- The adept's discipline: indefatigable labour at his own expense, learning from error, book interpreting book, note-keeping, constant meditation — “What was wrong taught me what was right” [IV.1 ¶29; IV.1 n24].
- A detailed account of the first act and the Second Operation: “In the first act of the physico-chemical works, explains Khunrath” [IV.1 ¶36; IV.1 n29].
- An epigraph (“Enigma”) on a first-second-third transmission that introduces the threefold order: “Omnia in omnibus primum, omni Tertio traditit” [IV.2 ¶2].
- He is named among Adepts linking the work to the Creed, and is her main authority for the Stone's universal virtues, the Azoth and the fermentation with its metal; rightly conceiving the azoth is half the work. “It is the universal medium of restoration and preservation” [IV.3 ¶27; IV.3 ¶28; IV.3 ¶29; IV.3 n8; IV.3 n9].

**In the Appendix** (Table Talk, a later layer): he names the preserved principle of body (Caput Mortuum) “‘our pigmy’, also the ‘diadem of the body’”, and Atwood thinks he also calls it Duanach [APP ¶26]. He teaches that the Art perfects the mineral life and typifies the Divine; with Grsaeus he insists on the Stone/Christ analogy, which Atwood defends as “more than pardonable” [APP ¶44; APP ¶46]. She compares him for Behmen's law: “the Enigma Omia in omnibus” [APP ¶73].

E0927.summary: In Maria's words, the soul and spirit: two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body.
E0927.body: In a passage quoted from Maria, “Kibric and Zibeth (the soul and spirit)” are “the two fumes which comprise and embrace each other in the two luminaries”; they are two fumes of one root, the root of the Hermetic science, rectified upon the white body [I.3 n67].

E0928.summary: A figure for the ruling principle: the Rational Efficient, the soul as man's centre, and the source of the soul's faculties, held captive until it is restored.
E0928.body:
**Atwood.** In a note, the crowned speaker chained to his mother, who makes occult matter appear, is explained: “By the king, the Rational Efficient is signified” [I.3 n50]. She observes that the adepts keep his secret and “make little or no mention of the king at all” [II.1 ¶7]. In Part IV the soul's faculties are “engaged voluntarily in the restitution of their King”, “for the sake of him who is their source”, who is otherwise held in “an illegitimate thralldom under all”; he is renewed together with his ‘brethren’ [IV.4 ¶20].

**Sendivogius.** The King is the soul in man, his centre, seated in the vital spirit in the purest blood: “the soul in man, the lesser world or microcosm, substituting the place of its center, is the king” [II.1 ¶10].

**The Hunting of the Greene Lyon** (quoted). The King is the child of Sun and Moon wedded by the Lion: “And yet thys King was begott by none other, But by Sun and Moone hys owne Sister and Brother.” He is fed on the Lion's Blood, dies (paired with blackness) and rises, and is fed with Luna if white, the Sun if red [III.1 ¶65]. The same sequence calls the matter ‘this young Chylde’ or ‘Child’; the text does not say outright that King and Child are the same.

The readings fit together (rational principle, soul as centre, source of the faculties), but the text does not join them explicitly.

E0929.summary: Cited in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710.
E0929.body: Atwood cites the king of Prussia in support of a transmutation at Berlin in 1710 [I.1 ¶77; I.1 n104].

E0930.summary: Glossed by Atwood: Hermes means the great Law of Light or universal reason, impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature.
E0930.body: Atwood explains it in a note: “By the King’s seal, Hermes signifies the great Law of Light or universal reason”, which is impressed on the regenerated vitality of nature [I.3 n69].

E0931.summary: Correspondent in the *Theos. Correspondence*, cited in the Appendix with approval on the physical problem and the Divine Will, but criticized as a seeker who did not wholly convert into the Light.
E0931.body: All citations are in the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer). From the *Theos. Correspondence*, p. 168, Atwood takes the naming of ‘the physical problem’, making the invisible spirit visible [APP ¶93]. From p. 236 she endorses: “the Divine Will makes use of the human voice as an organ for conducting the Light, through the fire”, glossing the fire as our chaotic will [APP ¶97]. From p. 359, said “for de St Martin”: “there is no true government but a Theocracy”, which she calls a great truth but qualifies. She criticizes Kirchberger himself as an intellectual seeker who did not convert wholly into the Light [APP ¶112; APP ¶114].

E0932.summary: Cited for alchemy's antiquity, for a Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies, and for a transmutation story.
E0932.body: Atwood cites A. Kircher (*Oedipus Aegyptiacus*; *de Lapide Philos. Dissert.*) in support of alchemy's antiquity, and as the source of the Latin rendering of the Smaragdine Table from Arabic and Greek copies [I.1 ¶3; I.1 n2; I.1 ¶7]. His *Mundus Subterraneus* supplies an explicit transmutation story [I.1 ¶77].

E0933.summary: An adept and commentator on Basil Valentine, whose Latin version underlies the only good English Valentine; cited on the key and on prayer in the work.
E0933.body: Atwood calls Kirchringius ‘the adept’ and his commentaries ‘useful’ [I.1 ¶27]. His Latin version of Valentine, with its ‘admirable commentary’, is the basis of the only good English translation [I.1 ¶61]. She cites him with approval: the key is the principal part of the Art, and “this opens the first gate, this will also unlock the last”; its method is called Manual Operation [III.1 ¶37]. From his *Annotations* on Basil Valentine she takes the efficacy of prayer, both in the work and in solving enigmas: prayer as desire plus cooperation, yielding revelation — “even in the midst of the operations of Vital Chemistry, full of labour and toil, they prayed, says Kirchringius” [III.4 ¶22; III.4 n24].

E0936.summary: Author of *des Cieux*, criticized by Atwood for an agricultural interpretation.
E0936.body: Atwood criticizes La Pluche (*des Cieux*) for an agricultural interpretation [II.2 ¶4; II.2 n3].

E0937.summary: Atwood's term for man himself as the true place of the Hermetic work.
E0937.body: Atwood concludes that the work's place is man: “Man then, shall we conclude at length, is the true laboratory of the Hermetic art” [II.1 ¶30]; “Man was the proper laboratory of the whole Art” [IV.4 ¶3].

E0938.summary: Cited in support of a prophecy's authenticity, since he mentions it without doubt.
E0938.body: Atwood cites Lactantius in support of the prophecy's authenticity, since he mentions it without doubt [I.1 ¶11].

E0939.summary: A name for the Matter as latent in and about all things, celebrated by ‘the Enigma’; the text does not explain it further.
E0939.body: Atwood speaks of “the alone Laelia Aelia latent in and about all, which the Enigma celebrates as comprehending all” [I.2 ¶34]. The context suggests a name for the Matter; the text does not explain it further.

forms: Land of Promise of the Wise
E0940.summary: In Eudoxus' words, the fertile earth into which the mercurial water is turned, on which the wise make the dew of Heaven fall.
E0940.body: Quoting Eudoxus: the mercurial water is turned into an earth on which the wise make the dew of Heaven fall: “An earth admirable is it for fertility -- the Land of Promise of the Wise” [IV.3 ¶12].

E0941.summary: A name for the Matter as liquid, equated by the quoted authorities with the sharp vinegar and blessed water, which the alchemical reduction uncovers.
E0941.body: In a passage given from Synesius and the New Light: “this Latex is the sharp vinegar which makes gold a pure spirit, seeing she is even that blessed water which engenders al things” [I.2 ¶33]. The Alchemists seek “such a reducation of nature as shall discover this Latex without destroying her vehicle, but the modal life only” [II.1 ¶47]; this passage does not define it further.

E0942.summary: Unattributed Latin maxims that Atwood cites in support: only one who has it can give it, and the end depends on the beginning.
E0942.body: “Nemo enim dat id, quod non habet.” (ours: For no one gives what he does not have) supports her point that only one who has it can impart it [II.2 ¶29]. “Sie finis ab origine pendet.” (ours: So the end hangs from the beginning) supports her point that the Motive governs the result [IV.1 ¶45].

E0943.summary: The union of Altitude and Profundity at their extreme poles, by which the wheel of Life is turned.
E0943.body: Atwood: “Altitude and Profundity, being united at their extreme poles, make Latitude”, and by it the wheel of Life is turned [III.3 ¶72].

E0945.summary: The intelligible law of reason or soul, whose revelation is the soul's own self; in the Kabalist's sense, the scriptural Law, whose real substance is its Soul.
E0945.body:
**Atwood.** The perfected soul, “percipiently included in the circular necessity of her Law, believes its revelation which is her very self” [II.3 ¶46]. The wisely simple are those “who have subdued their will to the Law of Wisdom” [II.3 ¶55].

**The Kabalist (endorsed by Atwood).** The scriptural Law has an outer story that clothes it: “The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law”, and each word cloaks a sublime mystery “under the Bark of the Law”. Its real substance is its Soul: “the Soul, which is the basis of all rest; which is the Law itself” [III.3 ¶59].

E0946.summary: What the priests forsook when they tried to wield magic power without it, which led to confusion.
E0946.body: Atwood says the priests, “having forsaken the law of conscience, attempted to wield without it the rod of magic power”, which led to confusion [I.1 ¶30].

E0947.summary: Behmen's law: an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself; the Hermetic Work follows the same order.
E0947.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer): “The Law of Divine Manifestation is expressed in those striking words of Behmen” — an Eternal Will arises in the No Thing to bring it into Something, so that the Will might behold itself. Atwood says the Hermetic Work follows the same order [APP ¶73].

E0948.summary: Where, Atwood says, ‘the strength of sin’ lies; the text does not explain it further.
E0948.body: Atwood: “the strength of sin is in the Law of dual generation” [III.2 ¶62]. The text does not explain it further.

E0949.summary: The law that exacts exact retribution (‘eye for an eye’) in the spheres of the work.
E0949.body: Atwood: “so does the Law of Justice exact retribution in those spheres”, that is, an eye for an eye [III.4 ¶9].

E0950.summary: A law that must move through Love in the will; for the Kabalists, the superstantial law from which the world emanates as an efflux of Mind.
E0950.body:
**Atwood** (Appendix, Table Talk, a later layer): “there is a law of Light, which must move through Love in the will” and act on the will-moved mind; the mind must be subservient to it or become demoniacal [APP ¶9].

**Hebrew Kabalists** (reported): in their Idealism “the whole world was before their eyes as an efflux of Mind, an emanation of the great superstantial Law of Light” [II.1 ¶40]. Compare King's seal, glossed as “the great Law of Light or universal reason” [I.3 n69].

E0951.summary: Nature's simple and harmonious law, which baffles the operator who brings his own blind purpose; the moral, physical and organic laws are one at the root.
E0951.body: Atwood: “The Law of Nature, being simple and harmoniously framed, will baffle him” — the operator who brings his own blind purpose is baffled and condemned [III.1 ¶38]. The Laws of Nature — “the moral, the physical, and the organic are well reasoned, as in their constitutional consequences, apart from each other” — seem independent at nature's circumference but are one at the root [III.4 ¶8].
